constraint_checks.constraint_notes: All agents are human professional or social roles; only the agent varies across sentences; all can physically perform the action, so plausibility depends on role–action mismatch.

plausible_easy.reasoning: Measuring blood pressure with a cuff in a medical examination room is a canonical nursing task and likely the default expectation in this setting.

counter_arguments.argument_for_higher: N/A for plausible_easy since it is the highest level
counter_arguments.argument_for_lower: One could argue that in some practices doctors or medical assistants also take vitals, so a nurse is only one of several plausible professionals rather than uniquely prototypical; however, in many healthcare systems, nurses (or nurse-like roles) are strongly associated with taking blood pressure in exam rooms, so they remain the best choice for the highest plausibility level.

plausible_hard.reasoning: Paramedics routinely measure blood pressure but are more typically associated with ambulances and emergency scenes than with routine medical examination rooms, making this a plausible but less expected scenario.

counter_arguments.argument_for_higher: Since paramedics are trained medical professionals who frequently measure blood pressure, some viewers may treat any clinical-looking room as an acceptable setting and see this as almost as normal as a nurse performing the task.
counter_arguments.argument_for_lower: One could argue that paramedics normally operate in ambulances or emergency departments, so encountering one in a quiet examination room taking a routine blood pressure might feel odd enough to reject as unrealistic; however, paramedics can reasonably appear in hospital/clinic rooms during transfers or emergencies, so the event remains ultimately acceptable rather than clearly wrong.

implausible_hard.reasoning: A dentist is a clinical professional who treats human patients but typically works in a dental operatory and focuses on oral health, so seeing a dentist in a generic medical examination room taking blood pressure with a cuff feels related yet wrong for this specific scene.

counter_arguments.argument_for_higher: Dentists receive medical training and in some practices check patients’ blood pressure before procedures, so one might argue that extending this behavior to a more generic exam-room context is not entirely unreasonable and could be judged as an unusual but plausible clinical scenario.
counter_arguments.argument_for_lower: From a lay perspective, dentists are strongly associated with teeth and dental chairs, not with arm cuffs or general medical examination rooms, so a viewer might instantly reject the scene as absurd without much hesitation, especially if the image highlights distinctly dental gear.

occupational_domain.reasoning: Both nurses and dentists are healthcare professionals working in human medicine/clinical care.

typical_setting.reasoning: Both normally work in small clinical rooms with medical equipment, cabinets, and examination or procedure chairs, even if one is a dental operatory and the other a general exam room.

tools_instruments.reasoning: Both routinely use medical disposables (gloves, masks), sometimes syringes and monitoring devices, even though their specialized tools (dental drill vs. BP cuff) differ.

patient_object_type.reasoning: Both treat human patients directly, performing procedures on the body (general vs. oral).

physical_actions.reasoning: Both perform close, hands-on examinations and precise manual procedures on patients, often while standing beside a seated or reclined patient.

overlap_audit.negative_test: Even ignoring the act of measuring, a dentist in a clinical room with a patient has a clear association with the healthcare domain and patient-care context; the mismatch is that this is a general medical exam room and a blood-pressure task rather than a dental operatory and oral procedure, so the association persists but remains specifically wrong for this scene.

implausible_easy.reasoning: A ballet dancer has no professional connection to medical examinations, blood pressure monitoring, or clinical environments, so this combination is immediately implausible.

counter_arguments.argument_for_higher: One might imagine a dancer who has received some basic first-aid training and happens to help measure someone’s blood pressure, but this is highly contrived and not part of the ballet dancer role itself.
counter_arguments.argument_for_lower: N/A for implausible_easy since it is the lowest level

plausible_easy.reasoning: Scrubs, ID badge, and stethoscope form a highly recognizable ‘nurse/medical staff’ appearance.

plausible_hard.reasoning: An EMS-style uniform with reflective strips and patches is strongly associated with paramedics/EMTs.

implausible_hard.reasoning: A white dental coat, mask, loupes or headlamp, and a small dental mirror make ‘dentist’ readily guessable.

implausible_easy.reasoning: Leotard, tights, ballet slippers or pointe shoes, and a hair bun clearly signal a ballet dancer.

agent_appearances.plausible_easy: Typically wears solid-colored medical scrubs, comfortable clinical shoes, possibly an ID badge and a stethoscope around the neck, giving a generic nurse/clinical staff look.
agent_appearances.plausible_hard: Wears a dark EMS uniform with reflective stripes, service patches, duty belt or radio, and may carry or stand near an emergency medical bag.
agent_appearances.implausible_hard: Wears a white dental coat over scrubs or dress clothes, with a surgical mask (on face or pulled down), protective glasses or loupes, possibly a headlamp and a small dental mirror in hand.
agent_appearances.implausible_easy: Wears a fitted leotard with tights, ballet slippers or pointe shoes, hair in a tight bun, and optionally a light wrap skirt or warm-up sweater.

pe_vs_ph.note: Nurse in scrubs vs paramedic in dark EMS uniform with reflective strips and patches are visually distinct types of medical attire.

pe_vs_ih.note: Scrubs with stethoscope differ from a white dental coat with mask, loupes, and dental mirror.

pe_vs_ie.note: Clinical scrubs versus ballet attire (leotard, tights, pointe shoes) are drastically different.

ph_vs_ih.note: A dark EMS uniform with high-visibility elements is clearly distinct from a white-coated dentist with dental-specific gear.

ph_vs_ie.note: Paramedic uniform contrasts sharply with ballet performance clothing.

ih_vs_ie.note: Dental coat, mask, and instruments are entirely different from a ballet dancer’s leotard and pointe shoes.

scene_assessment.gradient_support_reasoning: All four agents were judged CORRECT for their assigned conditions, so no replacement agents are needed. The scene—a medical examination room with a blood pressure cuff—has a clear prototype (nurse), can accommodate a moderately plausible but less typical medical professional (paramedic), a related but wrong-domain clinician (dentist), and a completely unrelated role (ballet dancer).
scene_assessment.scene_notes: The blood-pressure measurement in a medical examination room is concrete and easy to depict, with a strong prototypical agent and enough domain structure to support the full plausibility gradient without relying on subtle or abstract reasoning.

overall.summary: This set cleanly instantiates the intended plausibility gradient for measuring blood pressure in a medical examination room, with a nurse as the prototypical agent, a paramedic as a less typical but plausible alternative, a dentist as a related but wrong clinician, and a ballet dancer as a clearly unrelated role. All four professions have strong, visually distinctive appearances, and the scene is straightforward to image and well-suited for the experiment’s rapid plausibility judgments.
